title: Yarn Types and Spinning Systems Compared
subtitle: Learn how ring, rotor, air-jet, friction, core-spun and filament yarns are made, and when to use each.
card_description: A free reading course comparing ring, rotor, air-jet, friction, core-spun and filament yarns: how each is formed, its structure and properties, and where it is used.

outcomes: Explain how yarn structure shapes strength, evenness, hairiness and handle
Describe how ring spinning inserts twist and why its speed is limited
Explain the open-end principle and compare rotor, air-jet and friction spinning
Describe how core-spun and filament yarns are made and used
Choose a suitable yarn type for a product and its end use
audience: Textile and fashion students, yarn and fabric buyers, merchandisers, and spinning, weaving or knitting staff who want to compare yarn types.
about: The same cotton can become a soft, fine shirting yarn or a firm, economical denim yarn, depending on how it is spun. This free reading course draws on two Fibre2Fashion articles by Dr Lipsa Mohapatra: “Yarn Properties and Applications of Ring-Spun, Rotor-Spun, Core-Spun and Filament Yarns” and “An Overview of Open-End Spinning: Rotor, Air-Jet and Friction Spinning”. You will see how ring, rotor, air-jet and friction spinning insert twist and build different yarn structures, and how core-spun and filament yarns add strength, stretch and engineered performance. It ends with a practical guide to choosing the right yarn for each end use.

lessons.title: The Open-End Principle and Rotor Spinning

quiz.q: What sets the speed ceiling of ring spinning?
options: Twist is inserted by rotating the whole yarn package
Fibres must first be separated into individual fibres
Wrapper fibres must be tightened by compressed air
It can only spin coarse counts
quiz.feedback: In ring spinning the rotating package inserts the twist, so package rotation and traveller speed cap output. Newer systems separate twist insertion from winding.

quiz.q: How does compact spinning improve on conventional ring spinning?
options: It feeds sliver directly, eliminating the roving stage
It wraps staple fibres around a filament core
It condenses the fibre strand before twist, reducing hairiness
It inserts false twist with swirling compressed air
quiz.feedback: Compact spinning condenses the fibre strand before twist insertion, so fewer fibre ends escape. The yarn is less hairy and can be stronger and more even.

quiz.q: In open-end spinning, how is twist inserted into the yarn?
options: By rotating the bobbin on a spindle
At the open end of the forming yarn, while the package only winds
By entangling continuous filaments with an air jet
By drafting roving between pairs of rollers
quiz.feedback: Fibres are separated, reassembled and twisted at the open yarn end. The package only winds, which allows higher delivery speeds and larger packages.

quiz.q: Air-jet spinning is a true open-end system, in the same way as rotor and friction spinning.
quiz.feedback: False. Air-jet spinning keeps the fibre strand continuous and wraps surface fibres around a core. It is grouped with open-end systems for its high productivity from sliver.

quiz.q: Compared with ring-spun yarn of a similar count, how does rotor-spun yarn generally differ?
options: It is stronger, softer and hairier
It is finer, smoother and more lustrous
It is weaker and less even, but softer
It is more even and less hairy, but weaker and firmer
quiz.feedback: Rotor yarn is more even, bulkier and less hairy, but usually 10–20 per cent weaker, with a firmer handle from its higher twist.

quiz.q: Which description fits the structure of air-jet yarn?
options: A core of nearly parallel fibres held by wrapper fibres at intervals
Fibres in helical paths, migrating between core and surface
A twisted core surrounded by irregular belt fibres
Continuous filaments with little or no twist
quiz.feedback: Air-jet yarn is fasciated: a largely untwisted, parallel core bound by wrapper fibres. This gives low hairiness but lower strength than ring yarn.

quiz.q: Which system's core-spinning capability supports heat-resistant yarns with aramid sheaths and conductive core yarns?
options: Compact ring spinning
Rotor spinning
Friction (DREF) spinning
Air-jet vortex spinning
quiz.feedback: Friction spinning, notably DREF-3, wraps fibres around a core strand. This supports technical yarns such as aramid-sheathed heat-resistant yarns and conductive core yarns.

quiz.q: Flat filament yarns have essentially no staple-fibre hairiness, because they contain no staple-fibre ends.
quiz.feedback: True. Their continuous structure gives a smooth, lustrous surface and low pilling, although they may snag depending on fabric construction.

quiz.q: A brand wants stretch denim that keeps a cotton-like surface. Which yarn suits it best?
options: Rotor-spun cotton yarn
Core-spun yarn with an elastane core and cotton sheath
Flat polyester filament yarn
Friction-spun DREF-2 yarn
quiz.feedback: In core-spun yarn the elastane core gives stretch, while the cotton sheath provides the surface handle, appearance and dyeability.

quiz.q: Which of these are typical uses of filament yarns? (select all that apply)
options: Linings and lingerie
Tyre cord and seat belts
Towels and heavy fleece
Hosiery and activewear
Blankets and filter fabrics
quiz.feedback: Flat filaments suit linings and lingerie, textured filaments hosiery and activewear, and high-tenacity filaments tyre cord and seat belts. Towels and blankets use staple-spun yarns.

glossary.def: A fibre of limited length, such as cotton, that must be twisted or wrapped with others to form a yarn.
A thick, untwisted rope of staple fibres. Rotor, air-jet and friction spinning work directly from it.
A thinner, slightly twisted strand drafted from sliver, which feeds the ring spinning frame.
Fibre ends protruding from the yarn surface. Excessive hairiness can contribute to pilling, fly and surface irregularity.
Spinning in which fibres are separated, reassembled and twisted at the open yarn end, while the package only winds.
Surface fibres wound around a yarn core, as in rotor yarn, where they are called belts, and air-jet yarn.
A yarn with a core of nearly parallel, largely untwisted fibres bound by wrapper fibres at intervals, as made by air-jet spinning.
Temporary twist that builds up before a twisting point and cancels out after it, leaving no net twist.
A yarn with a continuous filament core, such as polyester or elastane, covered by a staple-fibre sheath.
Processes such as false-twist and air-jet texturing that add crimp, loops or bulk to filament yarns.
